task.description: WF-03 Step 2 GATE for ISS-0446: validate CODE-DESIGNER's design (lib/letflow/design/iss0446-throwaway-supervisor-teardown-race-fix.md) against five load-bearing claims -- (1) the core structural-safety claim of link-propagated teardown, (2) CHECK 6 / no-coverage-loss, (3) name-leak under async/partitioned runs, (4) the rejected-option (d) reasoning, (5) the verification plan's soundness -- plus the standard no-implementation-code / unambiguous-for-ELIXIR-DEV checks.

result.summary:
FAIL. One BLOCKER. Independently re-derived all five load-bearing claims against real ExUnit 1.20.3/OTP source and empirical probes (not accepted on the strength of either upstream agent's argument, per this run's mandate).

ITEM 1 (core safety claim) -- CONFIRMED, holds up under adversarial testing. Read runner.ex:433-467 (spawn_test/3 -> spawn_test_monitor/4 -> exit(:shutdown) inside the test process, then receive_test_reply blocks the RUNNER process, then exec_on_exit runs the callback in a THIRD, freshly spawned process via on_exit_handler.ex's ensure_alive_callback_runner) and confirmed byte-for-byte against the design's and ISSUE-FIXER's citations. Read supervisor.ex:733's start_link/2 -- Elixir's own doc comment states explicitly: 'a supervisor started with this function is linked to the parent process and exits not only on crashes but also if the parent process exits with :normal reason' -- an OTP-documented guarantee, not a probabilistic timing effect. Ran an adversarial empirical probe (20 iterations) with a supervised child that TRAPS EXITS and sleeps 50ms in terminate/2 (deliberately worse than ISSUE-FIXER's own 5ms probe) and NO on_exit callback at all, modeling exactly ExUnit's real teardown shape (spawn a process, register a Supervisor.start_link'ed named supervisor + named child inside it, then exit(:shutdown)): 20/20 clean, both supervisor and child dead within the poll window every time. This corroborates the design's claim that removing the second actor (the on_exit callback process) removes the race structurally, not merely narrows it -- there is no scenario found where the supervisor outlives the test process's own exit signal.

ITEM 2 (CHECK 6 / no coverage loss) -- CONFIRMED. Independently re-read test/letflow/engine/service_task_dispatcher_test.exs:1113-1143 directly (not the design's quotation of it): the four assertions, the exact on_exit block text, line 35's async: false, and that the module's closing `end`s immediately follow line 1141 (file is 1143 lines total) all match the design's claims verbatim. Independently re-ran grep -rn "ThrowawaySupervisor" against the whole repository (not just test/): exactly one source-code hit, test/letflow/engine/service_task_dispatcher_test.exs:1128 -- the design's grep claim holds.

ITEM 3 (name-leak / partitioning) -- CONFIRMED, and the design's own reasoning is more defensible than a naive reading suggests. Read scripts/test_parallel.sh: mix test --partitions N splits test FILES across N separate OS processes (MIX_BUILD_PATH="_build/test-partition-$i" per partition), each a fully separate BEAM VM -- so a module-qualified atom name like __MODULE__.ThrowawaySupervisor occurring in exactly one file cannot collide across partitions regardless of this on_exit's presence or absence. Within a single partition/VM, async: false plus ExUnit's own runner serialization (verified directly in runner.ex above: receive_test_reply blocks until :test_finished, exec_on_exit runs before the next test is dispatched) is the actual ordering guarantee, independent of whether this callback exists -- the design states this correctly and does not overclaim that the on_exit itself was ever what prevented a collision.

ITEM 4 (rejected-option-(d) reasoning) -- BLOCKER, false premise found. The design's stated reason for rejecting (d) is that `start_supervised!/2` 'returns only the started child's pid' under a framework-owned supervisor, and that 'there would be no sup_pid to call Supervisor.which_children/1 on,' concluding (d) is only obtainable by either weakening the which_children/1 assertion or inventing an unprecedented new construction. This is FALSE. `ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor/0` (ex_unit.ex, @doc since: "1.11.0", public and documented: 'Fetches the test supervisor for the current test... This is the same supervisor as used by ExUnit.Callbacks.start_supervised/2') returns exactly the supervisor pid `start_supervised!/2` registers children under -- the design's own step-01 input handoff even cites `ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor()` by name (callbacks.ex:568-580) but stops short of checking whether it is independently callable from test code. Verified empirically: a throwaway ExUnit test calling `{:ok, sup} = ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor()` followed by `ExUnit.Callbacks.start_supervised({Poller, []})` and then `Supervisor.which_children(sup)` returns `[{Poller, pid, :worker, [Poller]}]` -- the exact `{module, pid, :worker, modules}` shape this test's own assertion already checks, with zero coverage loss and zero new construction (fetch_test_supervisor/0 is an existing, already-cited, 1.11.0-vintage public function). This combines start_supervised!'s structural monitor-based teardown immunity (on_exit_handler.ex's terminate_supervisor/2 -- Process.monitor + blocking {:DOWN,...} receive, no Process.alive? check at all) with full which_children/1 coverage, which is a strictly better outcome than option (a) on every axis the design itself uses to judge (a) as sufficient: same or smaller diff (removes the on_exit block AND the explicit Supervisor.start_link/name plumbing, replacing it with two well-precedented ExUnit calls), no coverage loss, and additionally removes item 1.2's accepted residual risk ('no fixture-level teardown of sup_pid remains... implicit, driven by the link... if a future edit changes start_link to start, this implicit cleanup silently stops working and nothing will detect it structurally') since start_supervised's teardown is framework-guaranteed rather than link-hygiene-dependent. Section 1.1's verdict ('(a) achieves full structural safety... with a strictly smaller diff... (d)'s structural-immunity mechanism is real and stronger in the abstract, but it is not available to this test without weakening the exact assertion') rests on a checkable factual premise that does not hold, per HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md Section 1.1's own rule that a handoff's factual premises must be verified, not inherited. This is a BLOCKER, not a stylistic quibble: the design chose an option specifically because a stronger, differently-mechanised option was believed unavailable, and it is in fact available with no coverage cost. An ambiguous-but-passable design is not the failure mode here -- a design that reasoned to the wrong answer from a false premise is exactly what this gate exists to catch before ELIXIR-DEV builds the weaker fix.

ITEM 5 (verification plan) -- Provisionally sound, not independently re-run to exhaustion this pass since Item 4 already fails the gate outright: the widened-timing-analog approach (a supervised child whose terminate/2 sleeps, run pre-fix and post-fix, non-committed scratch script) is methodologically the right shape for a race that does not reproduce on demand under quiet conditions -- confirmed by this validator's own adversarial probe (above) using the same technique successfully distinguishing behavior. Section 4.3's caveat that ordinary green runs are not evidence is correct and well-reasoned. No defect found here, but re-evaluate once rework addresses Item 4, since a rework that switches to fetch_test_supervisor/0 + start_supervised! would need this section restated for the new fixture shape (the widened-timing child would then be registered via start_supervised! rather than a bespoke Supervisor.start_link, and the design should confirm the same widening technique still applies to that path).

OTHER GATE CHECKS: No implementation code present -- confirmed by inspection, no elixir/ex fenced code blocks, prose and a markdown table only. Unambiguous for ELIXIR-DEV -- section 3's five-item instruction list is concrete and mechanical for option (a) as specified, but this is moot given Item 4 requires the design to be reworked toward a different (or explicitly re-justified) option before ELIXIR-DEV should build from it.

VERDICT: FAIL. One BLOCKER (Item 4's false premise about start_supervised!/ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor unavailability). Not close enough to pass on the theory that ELIXIR-DEV could work around it or that option (a) is 'good enough anyway' -- core-directives.md's humanless-pipeline principle and this role's Forbidden section both bar approving a design because it is close, and the whole point of comparing (a) against (d) explicitly was to make a real choice on real premises; those premises were wrong.

issues.description: Section 1.1's rejection of option (d) (start_supervised!/1) rests on a false premise: it claims start_supervised!/2 'returns only the started child's pid' with 'no sup_pid to call Supervisor.which_children/1 on,' and concludes (d) can only be adopted by weakening the which_children/1 assertion or inventing an unprecedented construction. This is incorrect -- ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor/0 (public, @doc since 1.11.0, already cited by name in ISSUE-FIXER's own Step 1 diagnosis at callbacks.ex:568-580) returns the exact supervisor pid start_supervised!/2 registers children under, and Supervisor.which_children/1 called on that pid returns the same {module, pid, :worker, modules} shape this test already asserts. Verified empirically in this gate: {:ok, sup} = ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor(); pid = ExUnit.Callbacks.start_supervised!({Child, []}); Supervisor.which_children(sup) returns [{Child, pid, :worker, [Child]}] with no coverage loss and no new pattern. Rework: CODE-DESIGNER must re-evaluate option (d) using ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor/0 to obtain the supervisor handle, and either (i) adopt this combined approach (start_supervised!/1's structural monitor-based teardown immunity, per on_exit_handler.ex's terminate_supervisor/2, plus full which_children/1 coverage via the fetched supervisor -- strictly better than option (a) on every axis the design itself uses: equal-or-smaller diff, zero coverage loss, and removes 1.2's accepted residual link-hygiene risk since teardown is framework-guaranteed rather than link-dependent), or (ii) if CODE-DESIGNER identifies a concrete reason this combined approach is unsuitable that this gate's probe did not surface (e.g. an ordering/isolation concern with other start_supervised! usages elsewhere in this same test file, though none currently exist), state that reason explicitly and re-justify (a) against the corrected premise rather than the false one.
